intro: About 60 items in about 120 minutes, pass mark 720/1000 (assumed), USD 99 at Pearson VUE. It tests everyday Claude use: judging outputs, fitting Claude into a workflow, responsible use, prompting, picking a model or capability, Projects and memory, and troubleshooting. Read each domain summary first, then the notes; the cards and the cram sheet are the recall drill.

domains.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A([Claude draft]) --> B{Every claim traceable?}
  B -->|No| C[Source it or remove it]
  B -->|Yes| D{All required parts covered?}
  D -->|No| E[Fill gaps or justify exclusions]

notes.objective: Verify factual accuracy and detect potential hallucinations in Claude-generated content before distribution or use.
notes.title: Trace every claim to a source
notes.gist: Confident wording is not evidence; a figure or claim leaves the draft only when you can point to where it came from.
points: Check each specific statistic, date, quote or citation against the source document or a trusted reference; tone and polish prove nothing.
Vague authority such as 'an established best practice' with no citation: flag it and require a named source or remove it.
Prompt-side guards: let Claude say it does not know, ask for word-for-word quotes first on long documents (over about 20k tokens), require a supporting quote per claim or a retraction.
Restrict Claude to the provided documents when the answer must come from them, not from general knowledge.
Running the same prompt several times and comparing (best-of-N) exposes unstable, likely fabricated details.
notes.tip: Stems say a figure 'will be cited directly' or a claim 'sounds authoritative'. The answer verifies against the source; options that judge by confidence, word count or structure are distractors.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Claim in Claude output] --> B{Source supports it?}
  B -->|Yes| C[Keep and cite]
  B -->|No| D[Flag: source it or remove it]
  D --> E[Never publish on tone alone]

notes.objective: Assess structural completeness and requirement alignment in Claude outputs to identify gaps or missing components.
notes.title: Check coverage against the requirements
notes.gist: Completeness means every required element and every critical source section is covered or deliberately excluded, not that the output looks finished.
points: Build a checklist from the original request and the source's major sections; mark each item covered or excluded with a reason.
A summary that hits the page count or reads well can still drop a critical requirement; length and compression ratio are not completeness checks.
Never accept Claude's own assurance that nothing was omitted; verification must be independent of the model.
Conflicting or incompatible requirements extracted from stakeholders are flagged back to the stakeholders to resolve, never merged or silently dropped.
A missing point in a three-part answer usually traces to a prompt that did not enumerate the parts explicitly.
notes.tip: 'Well-written and spot-checked accurate' is the setup; the answer compares source scope with summary coverage section by section. Claude self-assessment is always the wrong option.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Required elements list] --> B[Compare with the output]
  B --> C{Each item covered or justified?}
  C -->|No| D[Fill the gap or note the exclusion]
  C -->|Yes| E[Move to style and format review]

source.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

notes.objective: Evaluate and revise Claude-generated content to align with organizational style guides, terminology standards, and editorial requirements.
notes.title: Fix terminology at the source
notes.gist: When accurate output uses the wrong house terms, give Claude the style guide and glossary rather than editing every draft by hand.
points: Most direct fix for terminology drift: supply the style guide, glossary or approved-terms list in the prompt or Project instructions and regenerate.
Examples of approved output steer wording, tone and structure more reliably than abstract instructions.
Tell Claude what to do, not what to avoid: 'use the glossary terms' beats 'do not use jargon'.
A voice problem that recurs in every chat belongs in Project custom instructions so each conversation starts correct.
Editorial constraints (length, headings, citation style) are stated up front, then checked on review.
notes.tip: Options that edit by hand each time, 'accept the minor friction' or tell the team to adopt Claude's style are traps; the answer feeds the standard to Claude once.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Output uses off-standard terms] --> B[Add glossary and style guide]
  B --> C[Add one approved example]
  C --> D[Regenerate and compare]
  D --> E[Move rules into Project instructions]

notes.objective: Select appropriate output formats and structures that optimize clarity, scannability, and usability for intended stakeholders.
notes.title: Format for the reader
notes.gist: Pick the structure the audience will actually scan: lead with the decision, then supporting detail, in the form their workflow consumes.
points: Executives and busy stakeholders: headline conclusion first, short sections, key numbers visible; technical depth moved to an appendix.
Media or external audiences: core announcement, supporting details and company position immediately clear, in that order.
Match the medium: tables for comparisons, numbered steps for procedures, prose for narrative judgement; say which in the prompt.
Ask for an explicit format (headings, template, JSON) so output is consistent across runs; the prompt's own style nudges Claude's style.
An accurate but highly technical analysis bound for non-technical leaders is rewritten for them, not sent as is.
notes.tip: The stem names the audience and its constraint (non-technical, strict deadline, read on a phone). The right revision restructures for that audience; keeping every term 'for accuracy' is the trap.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A{Who reads it and how?} -->|Executives| B[Decision first, detail after]
  A -->|Operators| C[Numbered steps and checklists]
  A -->|Analysts| D[Tables and full data]
  B --> E[State the format in the prompt]
  C --> E
  D --> E

notes.objective: Establish quality assurance protocols by defining evaluation criteria and completing prerequisite activities before validating Claude outputs.
notes.title: Define the bar before you grade
notes.gist: Quality assurance starts with written, measurable criteria and the reference materials in hand; only then does validating a Claude output mean anything.
points: Good criteria are specific, measurable, achievable and relevant: 'F1 of at least 0.85 on 10,000 held-out posts', not 'classify well'.
Sequence: define criteria and gather sources, then check coverage and cross-check facts, then style and format, then sign-off and distribution.
Grading ladder: code checks (exact or string match) are fastest; a model judge with a clear rubric scales; human review is best but slow, so sample it.
Prefer many automated test cases over a few hand-graded ones, and include edge cases: irrelevant, overlong or ambiguous inputs.
Reporting a trial to a committee: lead with measured results against the agreed criteria plus the limits found, not anecdotes.
notes.tip: 'What is the proper sequence' questions put criteria and prerequisites first and distribution last. Any order that validates before criteria exist is wrong.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Write measurable criteria] --> B[Gather sources and references]
  B --> C[Validate the output against them]
  C --> D{Meets the bar?}
  D -->|No| E[Revise prompt or draft]
  D -->|Yes| F[Approve and distribute]

notes.objective: Apply the AI Fluency Framework's Discernment and Diligence competencies to systematically review and validate Claude-generated deliverables.
notes.title: Discernment judges, Diligence owns
notes.gist: Discernment is judging the product, process and performance of Claude's work; Diligence is doing it responsibly, transparently and with accountability for what you release.
points: The AI Fluency Framework has four competencies, the 4Ds: Delegation, Description, Discernment, Diligence.
Discernment has three lenses: product (is the output correct and fit), process (did Claude reason sensibly), performance (how the interaction went).
Diligence has three parts: creation (responsible choices while building), transparency (being open that AI was involved and how), deployment (owning the outcome you release).
Handle feedback systematically: ask reviewers to clarify vague comments, record which feedback drove which change, never apply contradictory feedback at once.
A claim that AI can fully replace human review of compliance documents is answered with evidence of limits and a human-owned sign-off, even to the budget holder.
notes.tip: 'Judging quality' maps to Discernment; 'accountability, transparency, ownership' maps to Diligence. Delegation and Description are the planning and prompting side.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Claude output] --> B[Discernment: product, process, performance]
  B --> C{Good enough?}
  C -->|No| D[Describe better and retry]
  C -->|Yes| E[Diligence: transparent, accountable release]

summary.tests: Whether you can tell a polished Claude output from a correct, complete, on-standard one, and run a defined review before anything is distributed.
must_know: Verify every specific claim, figure or citation against the source; confident tone, length and structure prove nothing.
Unsourced claims such as 'a widely accepted best practice' are flagged: name a source or remove them.
Completeness is checked by comparing the source's major sections and the original requirements with the output, item by item.
Conflicting extracted requirements go back to the stakeholders to resolve; never merge or drop them silently.
Terminology or voice mismatches are fixed by supplying the style guide and glossary (ideally in Project instructions), not by hand edits.
Define specific, measurable criteria and gather references before validating; then coverage, facts, style, sign-off.
4Ds: Delegation, Description, Discernment (product, process, performance), Diligence (creation, transparency, deployment).
traps: Accepting Claude's self-assessment that nothing was omitted instead of independent verification.
Judging accuracy by word count, section count, thesis quality or confident phrasing.
Rewriting terminology by hand every time instead of giving Claude the standard once.

cards.q: A Claude figure 'per the latest industry report' will be cited in a board deck. What first?
cards.a: Trace it to the actual source document or a trusted reference; if it cannot be substantiated, flag it and do not cite it.

cards.q: A report cites 'a widely accepted best practice' with no source. Reviewer action?
cards.a: Flag it as unverified and require a specific authoritative source or removal of the statement.

cards.q: How do you verify a 3-page summary of a 45-page manual is complete?
cards.a: List the source's major sections and critical requirements; confirm each is covered or deliberately excluded with justification.

cards.q: Extracted requirements contain two incompatible stakeholder requests. Responsible handling?
cards.a: Flag the conflict to the stakeholders to resolve; do not merge them, pick one silently or drop them.

cards.q: Accurate output uses terms that clash with the company lexicon. Most direct fix?
cards.a: Give Claude the style guide and glossary in the prompt or Project instructions and regenerate; do not hand-edit each draft.

cards.q: What makes a success criterion good in Anthropic's docs?
cards.a: Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant: for example F1 of at least 0.85 on a held-out set of 10,000 items.

cards.q: Order the QA steps: cross-check facts, define criteria, gather sources, distribute, check style.
cards.a: Define criteria, gather sources, check coverage and cross-check facts, check style and format, then distribute.

cards.q: Which grading method is fastest and most scalable, and which is best but slowest?
cards.a: Code-based grading (exact or string match) is fastest; human grading is highest quality but slow and expensive.

cards.q: Name the four AI Fluency competencies.
cards.a: Delegation, Description, Discernment, Diligence.

cards.q: What are the three lenses of Discernment?
cards.a: Product (is the output correct and fit), process (how Claude got there), performance (how the interaction went).

cards.q: What are the three parts of Diligence?
cards.a: Creation, transparency and deployment diligence: responsible building, openness about AI use, ownership of what you release.

cards.q: Two constructive ways to handle reviewer feedback on a Claude draft?
cards.a: Ask reviewers to clarify vague feedback before changing anything, and document which feedback item drove which revision.

cards.q: Trap: which signals wrongly suggest a Claude analysis is accurate?
cards.a: Confident tone, section count, word count, a strong thesis or varied sentences. Only source verification tests accuracy.

cards.q: Which prompt-side guards reduce hallucination?
cards.a: Let Claude say it does not know, ask for word-for-word quotes first, require a citation per claim or retraction, restrict to provided documents.

flowchart LR

notes.objective: Identify which tasks and process stages in knowledge work are most suitable for Claude integration based on impact potential and workflow characteristics.
notes.title: Pick stages Claude is good at
notes.gist: Claude pays off on high-volume, text-heavy work with clear inputs; it is a poor fit where the step is a judgement call someone must own.
points: Strong fits: drafting, summarising, consolidating documents, extracting and structuring information, first-pass classification and routing, converting between formats.
Weak fits: final decisions on people, money or compliance; live conversations that need relationship context; tasks with no written inputs.
Rank candidate stages by volume, time spent and how clearly the input and output can be described.
Anthropic's documented production use cases: ticket routing, customer support agents, content moderation, legal summarisation, commerce agents.
A generic 'typical improvement roadmap' without the organisation's own data is not a use case; it is a hallucination risk.
notes.tip: Two-answer questions pair one synthesis task with one structuring task as correct, and hide a human-judgement or relationship step among the distractors.

notes.objective: Conduct foundational planning activities including process mapping and stakeholder analysis before implementing Claude into operational workflows.
notes.title: Map the process before automating
notes.gist: Before any Claude step is added, document the current workflow and know who owns, feeds and is affected by each stage.
points: Process map first: inputs, steps, outputs, hand-offs, where time and errors concentrate; this is where delegation points become visible.
Stakeholder analysis: owners, operators, downstream consumers, compliance; capture their concerns before designing.
Define the core problem and its constraints before generating solutions; ideation on an undefined problem wastes effort.
Record the current performance metrics as a baseline so a pilot can be judged against something real.
Only then write prompts, Project instructions and the pilot plan.
notes.tip: 'Which should be completed first' in a solution-design stem is almost always 'define the problem, constraints and current process'; brainstorming, prototyping and evaluation come after.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Define problem and constraints] --> B[Map the current process]
  B --> C[Identify stakeholders and concerns]
  C --> D[Record baseline metrics]
  D --> E[Design the Claude-assisted flow]

source.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

notes.objective: Sequence the rollout of Claude integration into critical processes by first assessing stages, then piloting with monitoring, and finally scaling based on results.
notes.title: Assess, pilot, then scale
notes.gist: Roll Claude into a critical process in three gated stages, and let measured pilot results, not enthusiasm, decide the next step.
points: Stage 1 assess: which tasks Claude handles well and where humans must take over.
Stage 2 pilot: a small scope (one team, a subset of tickets) with monitoring, review sampling and a rollback path.
Stage 3 scale: expand only on pilot metrics against the baseline, after refining the workflow from pilot feedback.
Anthropic's guidance: start with the simplest solution and add complexity only when it demonstrably improves outcomes.
Keep human checkpoints for high-impact actions during and after the pilot.
notes.tip: Sequence questions list assess, pilot, refine and scale out of order; the answer starts with assessment and ends with scaling.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Assess stages and hand-offs] --> B[Pilot small scope with monitoring]
  B --> C{Metrics beat baseline?}
  C -->|No| D[Refine prompts and workflow]
  D --> B
  C -->|Yes| E[Scale in stages]

notes.objective: Evaluate and select workflow activities for Claude assistance by analyzing which steps are genuinely well-suited for AI support versus those requiring human judgment.
notes.title: Delegation: what Claude does, what you keep
notes.gist: The Delegation competency decides which parts of a task go to Claude, based on problem awareness, platform awareness and a clear split of responsibility.
points: Delegation has three parts: problem awareness (what are we really trying to do), platform awareness (what Claude can and cannot do), task delegation (who does which piece).
Delegate by two factors: how well the task can be specified and checked, and the cost of an error; not by how boring it is or by headcount targets.
Retain tasks that need accountability, confidential relationships or in-person judgement; Claude can still prepare materials for them.
Autonomous final approval of expense claims or loan decisions fails Delegation: a qualified human keeps the decision.
Delegation is not all-or-nothing; a stage can be 'Claude drafts, human approves'.
notes.tip: When the stem says 'AI Fluency Delegation competency', the answer weighs verifiability and error cost and keeps a human on consequential decisions.

notes.objective: Design Claude-assisted workflows by leveraging existing process documentation and performance metrics to identify optimization opportunities and appropriate delegation points.
notes.title: Use existing docs and metrics as inputs
notes.gist: Give Claude the documented process and its performance data, and ask it to find bottlenecks and candidate delegation points, with each finding traced to a source.
points: Feed documented process steps plus recent metrics (delays, error rates) and ask for a diagnosis with reasoning tied to the data.
Ask Claude to consolidate transcripts and documents into a process map with links back to the originals, so claims are auditable.
Improvements that count: fewer manual hand-offs, a reusable Project with instructions and reference documents, a validation step; not cosmetic changes.
Leadership cannot name the root cause? Have Claude analyse the documented data and surface hypotheses for humans to test, not guess.
Chained prompts with programmatic checks between steps turn a vague process into inspectable stages.
notes.tip: Options that have Claude invent a roadmap 'from typical strategies' or run the discovery interviews itself are wrong; the right ones ground Claude in the organisation's own documents and numbers.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Process docs and metrics] --> B[Claude maps steps and bottlenecks]
  B --> C[Findings linked to sources]
  C --> D[Humans choose delegation points]
  D --> E[Redesigned workflow with checks]

notes.objective: Prepare organizational change management for Claude integration by developing communication materials that address leadership and departmental stakeholder concerns.
notes.title: Communicate scope and limits honestly
notes.gist: Change-management materials say exactly what Claude will do, what stays with people and where it can fail; they are written after the process and pilot facts exist.
points: Before writing materials: finish the process assessment and the stakeholder analysis, and have pilot evidence to cite.
Leaders need: which tasks Claude assists, which decisions remain human, expected gains against the baseline, and the oversight plan.
Departments need: what changes in their day, who to ask, how errors are caught and escalated.
Never claim full autonomy, 'always accurate' or 'the system handles everything'; state known limitations plainly.
Expect the fear of replacement and answer it with the actual delegation split.
notes.tip: Two-answer stems pair 'transparent scope and human control' with 'candid limitations' as correct; vague or overclaiming statements are the distractors.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Assessment and pilot facts] --> B[Scope: what Claude does]
  B --> C[Boundaries: what humans decide]
  C --> D[Limits and oversight plan]
  D --> E[Tailor to leaders and departments]

notes.objective: Validate Claude integration readiness by confirming prerequisites such as data platform compatibility and security requirements before authorizing implementation.
notes.title: Confirm readiness before authorising
notes.gist: An integration is authorised only after the data, security and policy prerequisites are confirmed, not after the demo looks good.
points: Data readiness: the data Claude needs exists in a compatible, accessible form; sensitive fields are classified and masked or removed.
Security: who can access the Project, which connectors and tools are enabled, and whether code execution network egress is on or off.
Code execution runs in a sandboxed container; with network egress disabled, data cannot leave it even under prompt injection, so cautious rollouts start with egress off.
Policy: the use case is allowed by the governance framework and the Usage Policy; high-risk decisions keep a qualified human in the loop.
Agree monitoring, review sampling and a rollback path before go-live.
notes.tip: Readiness questions reward confirming compatibility and security requirements first; 'launch and fix later' or 'the pilot was fine so authorise' are traps.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A{Data accessible and classified?} -->|No| X[Not ready]
  A -->|Yes| B{Access, connectors, egress set?}
  B -->|No| X
  B -->|Yes| C{Policy allows, oversight set?}
  C -->|No| X
  C -->|Yes| D([Authorise implementation])

summary.tests: Whether you can decide where Claude belongs in a business process, plan and pilot it properly, and bring people along without overclaiming.
must_know: Claude fits text-heavy, repeatable, well-specified stages (drafting, summarising, structuring, first-pass classification); humans keep accountable decisions.
Define the problem and constraints, map the process, analyse stakeholders and record a baseline before designing or prompting.
Rollout order: assess stages and hand-offs, pilot a small scope with monitoring, refine, then scale on measured results.
Delegation = problem awareness, platform awareness, task delegation; decide by specifiability and cost of error.
Ground Claude in the organisation's own process documents and metrics, with findings linked to sources; never a generic roadmap.
Communications state scope, human control and limitations candidly; never 'fully autonomous' or 'always accurate'.
Readiness means data compatibility, access and egress controls, and policy approval are confirmed before authorisation.
traps: Letting Claude run discovery interviews or invent a roadmap instead of synthesising what humans gathered.
Piloting or writing communications before the process assessment exists.
Treating a good demo as readiness; skipping data classification and security configuration.

notes.objective: Identify and classify sensitive data types that require masking, removal, or careful handling before use with Claude.
notes.title: Know what counts as sensitive
notes.gist: Before data touches a prompt, classify it: identifiers, credentials and confidential records are handled or removed, public and non-sensitive material can flow.
points: Needs masking or removal: names tied to records, government or legal ID numbers, contact details, financial account data and credentials, health data, biometric data, confidential or proprietary information.
Fine to use: public regulatory filings, published product specs, role titles from a public directory, aggregated or anonymised figures.
The Usage Policy forbids misusing or collecting private information such as non-public contact details, health, biometric or confidential data without permission.
Classification is decided by the data owner or compliance role before the prompt is written, not by Claude at run time.
Appropriate data for an HR prompt: the task-relevant fields only, such as policy text and anonymised case descriptions.
notes.tip: Options listing public or already-disclosed information are the 'no special handling' distractors; the one with identifiers, credentials or health data is the one that needs protection.

notes.objective: Evaluate organizational AI governance frameworks to determine whether proposed Claude use cases comply with established policies and restrictions.
notes.title: Check the use case against the framework
notes.gist: A governance framework says which tools are approved, what data may be used, who approves and who is accountable; a proposed use either fits it or is declined and escalated.
points: A framework defines permitted tools, data boundaries, approval processes and accountability mechanisms for consistent use; it is not a price comparison or a training plan.
If policy prohibits Claude for active investigations or disciplinary matters, decline that use and point to the policy, even when a manager asks.
Anthropic's Usage Policy sits on top: universal standards plus requirements for high-risk areas such as legal, medical, finance, credit, insurance, housing, employment and education.
Outputs are yours to use in products and non-competing tools, but the terms prohibit using them to train models that compete with Anthropic's.
Commercial plans carry HIPAA-ready configuration (BAA), ISO 27001:2022, ISO/IEC 42001:2023 and SOC 2 Type I and II; documentation is on the Trust Portal.
notes.tip: Stems with a manager, executive or budget owner pushing a prohibited use test whether you follow the framework; the right option declines politely and routes through the proper channel.

notes.objective: Assess Claude implementation configurations for security, privacy, and responsible use alignment with organizational standards.
notes.title: Configure for privacy before sharing data
notes.gist: Protect sensitive conversations with the controls Claude already has: memory off or incognito, private Projects, restricted egress and vetted Skills.
points: Proprietary data in a one-off discussion: use an incognito chat (not saved to history or memory) or turn memory off for that chat before the first message.
Memory is per Project; turn off 'Use account memory' to keep a Project's memory fully separate; sensitive topics are not stored unless you opt in.
Team and Enterprise owners control whether memory, project sharing, public projects, code execution and network egress are available; HIPAA and custom-retention organisations do not get memory.
Keep client Projects private ('Only people invited'), one Project per client, and review Skills from unfamiliar sources before enabling: read bundled files, scripts and any network calls.
Legal and confidential work: commercial terms with no-training commitments, a professional visibly directing the work, and configuration reviewed with your own counsel.
notes.tip: Two-answer privacy questions pair incognito with per-chat memory off; options that 'assume brief mentions are not retained' or enable memory for continuity are wrong.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Sensitive session] --> B{One-off discussion?}
  B -->|Yes| C[Incognito chat or memory off first]
  B -->|No| D[Private Project, no account memory]
  C --> E[Review org controls: sharing, egress]
  D --> E

notes.objective: Apply data privacy protection measures including de-identification and removal of personally identifiable information from datasets before Claude processing.
notes.title: De-identify before the prompt
notes.gist: Strip or mask personal data before it is sent; an instruction to 'ignore the names' still puts the data into the system.
points: Remove fields the task does not need (ID numbers, addresses) before submitting; a technical-issue summary needs the issue text, not the customer's identity.
Swapping one identifier for a less sensitive one is still PII; use pseudonyms or tokens, not substitutions.
Interview transcripts: de-identify names, phone numbers and emails, then analyse; the insights survive without the identities.
Prompt instructions to exclude data from the output do not stop the data entering context and logs.
Privacy preservation can be a measured criterion, e.g. zero responses containing PHI across a 500-query test set.
notes.tip: The correct option removes or masks data before submission; 'include everything and tell Claude to exclude it' is the classic trap.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Raw dataset] --> B[Classify sensitive fields]
  B --> C[Remove what the task does not need]
  C --> D[Mask or pseudonymise the rest]
  D --> E[Send to Claude]

notes.objective: Determine appropriate levels of human oversight and decision-making authority when integrating Claude into business processes that affect compliance, HR, or financial outcomes.
notes.title: High-risk decisions keep a qualified human
notes.gist: Where an output affects someone's finances, employment, health, housing or legal rights, a qualified person reviews and owns the decision, and the person affected is told AI was involved.
points: Usage Policy high-risk areas: legal, medical, finance, credit, insurance, housing, employment, education and credentials, healthcare access, public benefits, legal adjudication.
Requirement: a qualified human meaningfully reviews the recommendation, with authority to change it, before it is delivered or acted on, and remains responsible.
Disclosure: the affected individual must be told AI was used; naming Claude or Anthropic is not required.
Exclusions: internal drafting, research or summaries that are not the final recommendation; wholly favourable decisions such as paying a claim may skip prior review where law allows.
So autonomous loan decisions, expense approvals or compliance verdicts are configured as 'Claude recommends, human decides'.
notes.tip: Any option that lets Claude 'autonomously render binding decisions' on loans, HR or compliance is wrong; pick the one that adds qualified human review and transparency.

flowchart TB
  A[Claude recommendation] --> B{High-risk area?}
  B -->|No| C[Normal review]
  B -->|Yes| D[Qualified human reviews, can change]
  D --> E[Human owns the decision]
  E --> F[Tell the affected person AI was used]

notes.objective: Communicate AI model capabilities and limitations to stakeholders to establish realistic expectations about Claude's role in organizational workflows.
notes.title: Set expectations with limits stated
notes.gist: Stakeholders get a plain statement of what Claude does well, where it fails and who checks it, so trust is calibrated rather than blind.
points: The limitation to lead with for production systems: Claude can produce fluent, confident output that is wrong, so verification stays in the process.
Claude can handle equations and calculations, but complex or mission-critical calculations should be verified with specialised software or by hand.
Answer 'AI can replace human judgement' with evidence of error modes and the human sign-off design, even when the speaker controls the budget.
Communicate scope (assists with X), boundaries (humans decide Y) and known failure areas; avoid 'always accurate' or 'handles everything'.
Diligence includes transparency: being open about where and how AI was used in a deliverable.
notes.tip: Correct options are specific and honest about both capability and limits; distractors overclaim autonomy or accuracy, or stay vague.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Stakeholder briefing] --> B[What Claude will do]
  B --> C[What stays human]
  C --> D[Known failure modes and checks]
  D --> E[Realistic expectations]

summary.tests: Whether you can keep sensitive data out of prompts, apply your organisation's and Anthropic's rules, keep humans accountable for high-stakes outcomes, and describe Claude honestly.
must_know: Sensitive: identifiers, credentials, contact, financial, health, biometric and confidential data. Public filings and published specs are not.
Remove or mask sensitive fields before submission; instructions to leave them out of the output are not protection.
A governance framework sets permitted tools, data boundaries, approvals and accountability; prohibited uses are declined even for senior requesters.

Usage Policy high-risk areas (legal, medical, finance, credit, insurance, housing, employment, education and more) need a qualified human reviewer with authority to change the decision, plus disclosure to the affected person.
Privacy controls: incognito chats, memory off per chat before the first message, private Projects, per-Project memory, organisation-level toggles.
Outputs may power your products but may not train competing models; Anthropic holds HIPAA-ready (BAA), ISO 27001, ISO/IEC 42001 and SOC 2.
Tell stakeholders the scope, the human boundaries and the failure modes; never 'fully autonomous' or 'always accurate'.
traps: Including the full record and asking Claude to leave identifiers out of the summary.
Letting Claude autonomously approve loans, expenses or compliance outcomes 'for efficiency'.
Assuming brief mentions of sensitive material are not retained by memory.

cards.q: Which data types need masking or removal before use with Claude?
cards.a: Personal identifiers, ID numbers, contact details, financial account data and credentials, health and biometric data, confidential or proprietary information.

cards.q: A ticket holds an ID number, address and a technical issue; you need an issue summary. Best practice?
cards.a: Strip the ID number and address before submitting; send only what the summary needs.

cards.q: Why is 'include everything but tell Claude to exclude the names' wrong?
cards.a: The data still enters the system and context; protection means removing or masking it before submission.

cards.q: What does an organisational AI governance framework establish?
cards.a: Permitted tools, what data may be used, required approval processes, and accountability mechanisms for consistent use.

cards.q: Policy forbids Claude for active investigations; a manager wants an investigation summary. Response?
cards.a: Decline that use, cite the policy, and route the request through the proper governance channel.

cards.q: Which areas does the Usage Policy treat as high-risk?
cards.a: Legal, medical, finance, credit, insurance, housing, employment, education and credentials, healthcare access, public benefits, legal adjudication.

cards.q: What two controls does the Usage Policy require for a high-risk AI recommendation?
cards.a: A qualified human reviews it with authority to change it before use, and the affected person is told AI was involved.

cards.q: A bank wants Claude to approve or deny loans with no human review. Responsible course?
cards.a: Keep a qualified human decision-maker: Claude recommends and explains, the human decides, with disclosure to applicants.

cards.q: Two privacy measures before discussing proprietary results with Claude?
cards.a: Use an incognito chat, or turn memory off for that chat before the first message.

cards.q: How is a Project's memory kept fully separate from other work?
cards.a: Each Project has its own memory; turn off 'Use account memory' on the Project page to keep it isolated.

cards.q: Can you use Claude's outputs to train your own models?
cards.a: Yes for non-competing tools and your own products; training models that compete with Anthropic's is prohibited.

cards.q: Which capability constraint should a team stress before a financial verification deployment?
cards.a: Claude can produce fluent, confident but incorrect output, so verification and human review must stay in the process.

cards.q: Which compliance credentials does Anthropic hold for commercial products?
cards.a: HIPAA-ready configuration with BAA, ISO 27001:2022, ISO/IEC 42001:2023, SOC 2 Type I and Type II.

cards.q: Trap: which stakeholder statements about Claude are inappropriate?
cards.a: That it works fully autonomously without oversight, is always accurate with no review, or 'handles everything' with no stated scope.

notes.objective: Clarify vague or underspecified requests through follow-up questioning to uncover actual user needs before sending prompts to Claude.
notes.title: Clarify the need before prompting
notes.gist: 'Analyse our market position' is not a task; ask what decision it serves, what evidence counts and what the deliverable looks like before writing the prompt.
points: Follow-up questions: purpose and decision, audience, scope (which competitors, which period), required evidence and format, deadline.
The real need is often narrower and factual, e.g. a sourced table of competitor prices with confidence levels, which calls for a research-style prompt with citations.
Description competency: describe the product (what you want), the process (how to approach it) and the performance (how to behave, e.g. ask when unsure).
Prerequisites before asking for messaging or content: the audience and the goal must be fixed and reference material gathered.
Anthropic's test: show the prompt to a colleague with no context; if they would be confused, Claude will be too.
notes.tip: When the stem reveals 'the actual need emerged' after conversation, the answer is the prompt that encodes that specific need (sources, confidence, format), not a generic analysis prompt.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Vague request] --> B[Ask: decision, audience, scope, evidence]
  B --> C[Restate the real need]
  C --> D[Write the specific prompt]
  D --> E[Colleague test]

notes.objective: Revise prompts to include sufficient context, constraints, and examples that enable Claude to produce complete, accurate responses across all requested elements.
notes.title: Task, context, constraints, example
notes.gist: A strong business prompt states the task precisely, gives the context Claude lacks, sets constraints and shows an example of the output you want.
points: Core components: an unambiguous task statement plus background (audience, objective, constraints); not product inventories, tone gimmicks or personal anecdotes.
Treat Claude as a brilliant new employee with no knowledge of your norms; explain why the task matters so it can generalise.
Examples (few-shot) are the most reliable way to set format, tone and structure; make them relevant, diverse and wrapped in example tags.
Structure with XML-style tags (instructions, context, input) and numbered steps where order matters; long documents at the top, the question at the end.
An audience line that does the work: 'for sales professionals with limited technical background, two pages maximum, end with three talking points'.
notes.tip: Given materials, a brand-voice sample and a target audience, the best option uses all three: attach the exemplar, name the audience, state the constraints. 'Maximum length' or 'preserve all jargon' are traps.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Task statement] --> E[Prompt]
  B[Context: audience, goal, why] --> E
  C[Constraints: length, format, scope] --> E
  D[Example of good output] --> E
  E --> F[Complete, on-target response]

notes.objective: Select and apply prompting methodologies (such as chain-of-thought, structured formats, or role-based prompting) that align with specific task characteristics and desired output types.
notes.title: Match the technique to the task
notes.gist: Role prompts set perspective, structured formats force consistency, step-by-step thinking helps reasoning and examples lock style; pick by what the task needs.
points: Role (a persona in the system prompt) when tone and perspective matter, e.g. 'senior compliance analyst'; even one sentence changes behaviour.
Structured output (template, JSON, XML, headings) when the result feeds a process or must be compared across runs.
Step-by-step reasoning or extended thinking for maths, multi-step logic and trade-off analysis; ask Claude to self-check against the criteria before finishing.
Examples for voice and layout; tell Claude what to do rather than what not to do.
In claude.ai: web search for quick current facts, extended thinking for hard reasoning without the web, Research for multi-source reports with citations (five or more tool calls, 1 to 3 minutes).
notes.tip: Map the stem's need to the technique: 'consistent structure' means a format template, 'nuanced reasoning' means thinking or chain-of-thought, 'specific perspective' means a role. 'Answer as a poem' is a distractor.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A{What does the task need?} -->|Perspective and tone| B[Role prompt]
  A -->|Consistent structure| C[Template or JSON format]
  A -->|Hard reasoning| D[Step-by-step thinking]
  A -->|Specific style| E[Examples]

notes.objective: Decompose complex, ambiguous requests into appropriately-scoped subtasks that balance granularity with coherence in Claude's responses.
notes.title: Decompose when deliverables differ
notes.gist: Split a request when it needs several distinct outputs or stages; keep it whole when it is one cohesive document from one set of inputs.
points: Signal to decompose: multiple distinct deliverables (segmentation analysis, campaign roadmap, success metrics) that can be refined independently.
Signal to keep whole: a single cohesive document, narrow scope, a standard template, or a request the team already handles in one prompt.
Chain prompts so each step's output feeds the next; you can inspect intermediate results and gate them. Common pattern: draft, review against criteria, refine.
Too fine a split loses shared context; too coarse hides where it went wrong. Subtasks are coherent units with clear inputs and outputs.
A twelve-rule instruction block that is randomly half-followed is a decomposition problem, not a wording problem.
notes.tip: 'What most strongly suggests decomposition' is answered by 'several distinct deliverables'; familiarity, narrow scope or a single document point the other way.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Complex request] --> B{Several distinct deliverables?}
  B -->|No| C[One well-structured prompt]
  B -->|Yes| D[Subtask per deliverable]
  D --> E[Chain: output feeds next step]
  E --> F[Check each step, then combine]

notes.objective: Identify and apply iterative prompt refinement techniques to improve output quality when initial responses are partially correct or incomplete.
notes.title: Refine one thing at a time
notes.gist: When output is partly right, diagnose which prompt element caused the gap, change that element and re-test against the same criteria.
points: Two of three requested points delivered: the prompt did not enumerate the required elements explicitly; list them and ask for each by name.
Change one variable per iteration and keep the version history; bundled edits hide what worked.
Use the output as input: ask Claude to verify or expand specific statements, or to review its draft against the criteria and revise.
Fresh, specific feedback ('section 3 lacks the cost comparison') beats repeating the whole prompt louder or expressing frustration.
Prerequisite for any refinement: success criteria and a way to test them; otherwise you cannot tell whether the change helped.
notes.tip: The best iterative option isolates the missing element and adds a precise instruction; 'regenerate and hope', 'rewrite from scratch' and 'make many edits at once' are distractors.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Partially correct output] --> B[Name the missing or wrong element]
  B --> C[Change that part of the prompt]
  C --> D[Re-run against the criteria]
  D --> E{Fixed?}
  E -->|No| B
  E -->|Yes| F[Lock the prompt version]

notes.objective: Maintain conversation productivity and clarity across extended multi-turn interactions by using organizational techniques such as summarization or context management.
notes.title: Keep long conversations productive
notes.gist: In a multi-week thread, recap decisions at breakpoints, restate scope when the phase changes, and migrate to a fresh chat or Project before the thread drowns.
points: At natural breakpoints, write a concise recap of decisions, trade-offs and open questions; it compresses working memory without losing what matters.
When pivoting to a new phase, restate its scope, success criteria and constraints so Claude is re-anchored.

Moving to a fresh chat: extract goals, decisions and remaining tasks first; then pick the materials to carry forward; put them in Project knowledge or attachments; start the new chat with the summary; verify.
Chat interfaces manage context first-in, first-out as it grows, and usage rises with conversation length; plan messages, batch related questions, refer back instead of repeating.
Memory and chat search let Claude pull prior context across sessions; Projects keep instructions and files persistent.
notes.tip: Two-answer stems pair 'recap at breakpoints' with 'restate scope on pivots'. A new thread for every phase, rapid topic switching and 'never condense' are the distractors.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Long conversation] --> B[Recap at breakpoints]
  B --> C[Restate scope on each pivot]
  C --> D{Thread hard to navigate?}
  D -->|Yes| E[Extract goals, start a fresh chat]
  D -->|No| B

summary.tests: Whether you can turn a vague request into a precise, well-structured prompt, pick the right technique, iterate deliberately and keep long conversations usable.
must_know: Clarify first: decision, audience, scope, evidence and format; the real need is often narrower and factual.
Strong prompt = unambiguous task + context (audience, goal, why) + constraints + an example; run the colleague test.
Technique by need: role for perspective, template or JSON for consistency, step-by-step thinking for reasoning, examples for style.
claude.ai capabilities: web search for quick facts, extended thinking for hard reasoning, Research for cited multi-source reports.
Decompose when there are several distinct deliverables; keep a single cohesive document whole; chain prompts so each step can be checked.
Refine one element at a time against fixed criteria; a missing point means the prompt did not enumerate it.
Long threads: recap at breakpoints, restate scope on pivots, migrate to a fresh chat or Project with a summary.
traps: Prompting a generic analysis when the clarified need was sourced facts with confidence levels.
Adding tone instructions, full product inventories or anecdotes instead of task, context and constraints.
Starting a new thread for every phase or refusing to condense history.

cards.q: A request says 'analyse our market position'. What do you do before prompting?
cards.a: Ask what decision it serves, the audience, scope, evidence and format; then write a prompt for that specific need.

cards.q: The clarified need is sourced competitor prices with confidence levels. Which prompt approach?
cards.a: A research-style prompt asking for factual, cited data per point with a confidence rating, in a fixed table format.

cards.q: Which two components belong in every strong business prompt?
cards.a: A specific, unambiguous task description and the context: audience, objective and constraints.

cards.q: What is Anthropic's colleague test for a prompt?
cards.a: Show it to a colleague with minimal context; if they would be confused, Claude will be too.

cards.q: Which technique fits 'consistent structure', 'nuanced reasoning' and 'specific perspective'?
cards.a: Template or structured format; step-by-step thinking; role prompt.

cards.q: When do you use web search, extended thinking or Research in claude.ai?
cards.a: Web search: quick current facts. Extended thinking: hard reasoning without the web. Research: multi-source cited reports, five or more tool calls.

cards.q: What most strongly signals a request should be decomposed?
cards.a: It requires several distinct deliverables, each of which can be refined independently.

cards.q: Claude answered two of three requested points. Which prompt part needs revision?
cards.a: The task specification: enumerate each required element explicitly and ask for all of them by name.

cards.q: Rule for iterating a prompt that is partly right?
cards.a: Change one element at a time, keep version history, re-test against the same criteria.

cards.q: Two strategies that keep a multi-week planning conversation productive?
cards.a: Recap decisions, trade-offs and open questions at breakpoints; restate scope, criteria and constraints when pivoting phases.

cards.q: First step when migrating a cluttered research chat to a fresh one?
cards.a: Extract the project goals, critical decisions and remaining tasks; then select materials, organise them, start the new chat, verify.

cards.q: Three parts of the AI Fluency Description competency?
cards.a: Product description (what you want), process description (how to approach it), performance description (how Claude should behave).

cards.q: Trap: which additions do not improve a campaign-brief prompt?
cards.a: Casual tone instructions, an inventory of every product line, or a personal anecdote to build rapport.

cards.q: Where do long documents go in a prompt, and what grounds the answer?
cards.a: At the top, above the question and instructions; ask Claude to quote relevant passages first.

notes.objective: Characterize the three Claude model tiers accurately in terms of their capabilities, performance characteristics, and appropriate use cases.
notes.title: Three tiers, three jobs
notes.gist: Haiku is fastest and cheapest for high-volume simple work, Sonnet balances speed and intelligence for everyday tasks, Opus is the most capable for complex reasoning and long autonomous work.
points: Haiku: lowest latency and price; classification, extraction, routing, real-time and high-volume processing, subagent tasks.
Sonnet: the best combination of speed and intelligence; code generation, data analysis, content creation, everyday agent work.
Opus: most capable, slower and dearest; complex reasoning, scientific and mathematical analysis, multi-hour agentic coding, accuracy over cost.

Capability and resource consumption rise together: a more capable tier costs more per token and responds more slowly. The current docs add Claude Fable above Opus for the most demanding work; exam questions use the three classic tiers.
All current models accept text and images, use tools and share a 1M-token context window; they differ in intelligence, speed and price, not in basic features.
notes.tip: 'Sophisticated analysis across interconnected variables' points to Opus; 'thousands of templated emails, minimise latency and cost' points to Haiku. 'All models are identical' is always false.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Haiku: fastest, cheapest] --> D[Simple high-volume tasks]
  B[Sonnet: balanced] --> E[Everyday analysis and content]
  C[Opus: most capable] --> F[Deep reasoning, long autonomy]

notes.objective: Select the appropriate Claude model tier based on task complexity, reasoning requirements, and processing volume; match model selection to operational requirements including response latency, throughput, and reasoning complexity for specific workflows.
notes.title: Choose by complexity, volume and latency
notes.gist: Start from the task's reasoning depth, its volume and its latency budget; then pick the cheapest tier that meets the quality bar and validate on real samples.
points: Two sanctioned starting strategies: efficiency-first (start Haiku, upgrade only for capability gaps) for prototypes, tight latency and cost-sensitive volume; capability-first (start Opus, optimise down later) for complex reasoning and accuracy-critical work.
Criteria to establish first: required capabilities, speed, cost and the effort level, which trades intelligence for latency and cost within one model.
A high volume of straightforward, templated messages: a Haiku-class model, validated by reviewing a representative batch before full rollout.
Routing pattern: send easy, common inputs to a small model and hard or unusual ones to a stronger model.
Asynchronous bulk jobs can use batch processing at a 50 percent discount; repeated prompt prefixes benefit from caching.
notes.tip: The answer names the tier and a validation step ('review a sample batch'). Picking the top tier 'because it is public-facing', rotating tiers weekly or copying last project's choice are traps.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A{Reasoning depth needed?} -->|High| B[Opus, then optimise down]
  A -->|Low or medium| C{High volume, tight latency?}
  C -->|Yes| D[Haiku, upgrade only on gaps]
  C -->|No| E[Sonnet]
  B --> F[Validate on real samples]
  D --> F
  E --> F

notes.objective: Evaluate model-to-task alignment decisions to determine whether selected models match specific capability and performance requirements.
notes.title: Judge alignment by the task
notes.gist: A model choice is justified when its capability profile matches the task's requirements; mismatches waste money (too big) or fail quality (too small).
points: Well-justified: Haiku for high-volume routing and extraction; Sonnet for everyday drafting and analysis; Opus for multi-step research or complex modelling.
Over-provisioned: Opus for templated confirmations or simple tagging; cost and latency with no quality gain.
Under-provisioned: Haiku for nuanced legal reasoning or long multi-document synthesis; expect misses and rework.
Review each decision against the stated requirements: accuracy bar, edge-case handling, latency and throughput, budget.
Switching models means re-testing prompts; a prompt tuned for one tier is not automatically right for another.
notes.tip: In 'which two selections are well-justified' questions, find the pairs where the stated workload matches the tier's sweet spot and reject any choice justified by prestige or habit.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Task requirements] --> B[Compare with tier profile]
  B --> C{Match?}
  C -->|Too much model| D[Downgrade, cut cost and latency]
  C -->|Too little model| E[Upgrade for quality]
  C -->|Fits| F[Approve with evidence]

notes.objective: Determine prerequisite activities and foundational work required before benchmarking and evaluating Claude models for critical applications.
notes.title: Before you benchmark
notes.gist: Benchmarking is only meaningful after you have written performance targets, picked candidates against them and built a representative test set.
points: Set targets first: output quality bar, acceptable latency, expected volume, budget.
Shortlist candidate models whose documented capabilities fit those targets.
Build benchmark tests specific to your use case from real prompts and data; a good evaluation set is the most important step.
Then compare accuracy, response quality and edge-case handling across models, and weigh performance against cost.
Approvals, production migration and re-validation on each model release come after testing, not before.
notes.tip: 'Which two must happen BEFORE pilot tests' is answered by targets plus a candidate shortlist; deployment, approvals and ongoing re-validation are later steps.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Define quality, latency, volume targets] --> B[Shortlist candidate models]
  B --> C[Build a representative eval set]
  C --> D[Run candidates on real samples]
  D --> E[Weigh performance against cost]

notes.objective: Identify use cases that align with Claude's core capabilities and strengths for organizational deployment.
notes.title: Use cases that fit Claude's strengths
notes.gist: Claude excels at reasoning over text and images, drafting, analysis and tool use; production guides exist for routing, support, moderation, legal summarisation and commerce agents.
points: Anthropic's documented use cases: ticket routing and classification, customer support agents, content moderation, legal document summarisation, commerce agents.
Strong fits in everyday work: summarising, drafting to a brief, structured extraction, comparing documents, explaining and translating between audiences.
Not a fit on its own: live facts without web search or Research, exact deterministic numbers without code execution, decisions that need accountability.
Claude can handle maths, but complex or mission-critical calculations should be verified with specialised software or manually.
Current models take text and images, support tool use and multilingual work; vision suits screenshots, charts and scanned documents.
notes.tip: Pick use cases where the input is text or images, the output is language or judgement, and a human owns the consequence. Beware options that treat Claude as a database or a calculator of record.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A{Input is text or images?} -->|No| X[Different tool]
  A -->|Yes| B{Output is language or judgement?}
  B -->|No| X
  B -->|Yes| C{Needs live data or exact maths?}
  C -->|Yes| D[Add search, Research or code execution]
  C -->|No| E[Core Claude use case]

notes.objective: Match model selection to operational requirements including response latency, throughput, and reasoning complexity for specific workflows, choosing the claude.ai capability that fits the job.
notes.title: Pick the right claude.ai capability
notes.gist: Beyond the model tier, claude.ai offers capabilities for specific jobs: Research for sourced reports, code execution for verifiable numbers and files, artifacts for interactive output, Projects for persistent context.
points: Research: searches and synthesises many current sources with citations; use for market landscapes, competitor comparisons, updating stale documents.
Code execution and file creation: runs code in a sandbox against uploaded data for reproducible calculations, charts and Excel, Word, PowerPoint and PDF output; 30 MB per file.
Artifacts display and let you edit substantial content (apps, documents, diagrams); they do not compute.
Web search for one or two quick facts; extended thinking for hard reasoning without the web.
Projects hold instructions and knowledge across chats; Skills package repeatable procedures; connectors reach external tools.
notes.tip: 'Verifiable numerical results from a spreadsheet' is code execution; 'current landscape with traceable citations' is Research; 'interactive view of results' is an artifact. Extrapolating from old data is always wrong.

flowchart TB
  A{What do you need?} -->|Sourced current report| B[Research]
  A -->|Exact numbers, files| C[Code execution]
  A -->|Editable interactive output| D[Artifact]
  A -->|One quick fact| E[Web search]
  A -->|Hard reasoning| F[Extended thinking]

Before benchmarking: define quality, latency and volume targets, shortlist candidates, build a use-case eval set from real data.
Routing sends easy inputs to a small model and hard ones to a strong model; batch processing is 50 percent cheaper for asynchronous bulk work.
Research for cited multi-source reports; code execution for reproducible numbers and files; artifacts for interactive output; web search for quick facts.
Documented use cases: ticket routing, support agents, content moderation, legal summarisation, commerce agents.
Complex or mission-critical calculations are verified outside Claude.
traps: Choosing the top tier for simple public-facing templates 'to be safe', or rotating tiers to balance cost.
Treating approvals or production migration as prerequisites to testing.
Using plain chat or extrapolation when the task needs current sourced data or deterministic computation.

cards.q: Characterise the three Claude tiers in one line each.
cards.a: Haiku: fastest and cheapest for simple high-volume work. Sonnet: balanced speed and intelligence. Opus: most capable for complex reasoning and long autonomy.

cards.q: Which tier for a forecasting problem with interconnected variables and deep analysis?
cards.a: Opus, the most capable tier, built for demanding reasoning.

cards.q: Thousands of templated confirmation emails per week, latency and cost critical. Choice and validation?
cards.a: A Haiku-class model, validated by reviewing a representative batch of outputs before full rollout.

cards.q: What is the relationship between model capability and resource consumption?
cards.a: They rise together: more capable tiers cost more per token and respond more slowly.

cards.q: Describe efficiency-first versus capability-first model selection.
cards.a: Efficiency-first starts with Haiku and upgrades only for gaps; capability-first starts with Opus and optimises down once it works.

cards.q: Two prerequisites before running candidate models on real workload samples?
cards.a: Establish performance targets (quality, latency, volume) and shortlist candidates aligned with those targets.

cards.q: What is the most important step when deciding whether to change models?
cards.a: Create a benchmark eval set specific to your use case, then test with your actual prompts and data.

cards.q: What is the routing pattern for cost optimisation?
cards.a: Send easy, common inputs to a smaller model and hard or unusual inputs to a more capable one.

cards.q: A market landscape with recent announcements, prices and regulations, all cited. Which capability?
cards.a: Research: it searches, aggregates and cites multiple current sources into a comprehensive report.

cards.q: Verifiable numerical results from a multi-sheet financial model. Which capability?
cards.a: Code execution: it runs calculations in a sandbox against the uploaded spreadsheet for reproducible outputs.

cards.q: What do artifacts do, and what do they not do?
cards.a: They display and let you edit substantial or interactive content; they do not perform computation.

cards.q: Which use cases does Anthropic document production guides for?
cards.a: Ticket routing, customer support agents, content moderation, legal summarisation and commerce agents.

cards.q: What does the batch API offer and when is it appropriate?
cards.a: A 50 percent discount on input and output tokens for asynchronous bulk jobs where latency does not matter.

cards.q: How should mission-critical calculations from Claude be handled?
cards.a: Verify them with specialised software or manual methods; Claude can compute but is not the system of record.

domains.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A([New Project]) --> B[Custom instructions: role, standards, format]
  B --> C[Add reference documents, clear names]
  C --> D[Set visibility: private or organisation]
  D --> E[Enable Skills for repeatable procedures]
  E --> F([Chats inherit instructions and memory])

notes.objective: Establish system-level instructions as the foundational step before implementing document-review workflows and other Project processes.
notes.title: Instructions first, workflows second
notes.gist: The first action in a new Project is writing the system-level custom instructions; every document-review or analysis workflow then inherits them.
points: Order: define the Project's purpose and custom instructions, then add knowledge, then run workflows; never the reverse.
Custom instructions apply to every chat in the Project, so tone fixes and recurring corrections belong there, not in the first message of each chat.
A Project that handles several data-processing workflows gets the shared system-level rules first, then per-workflow prompts.
Revisit configuration regularly: policies, terminology and reference materials change even while output still looks fine.
Research before engaging Claude: define the question, scope and success criteria, then gather sources into the Project.
notes.tip: 'What should be your first action' in Project setup is 'establish the custom instructions'; uploading documents or starting chats comes after.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Define purpose] --> B[Write custom instructions]
  B --> C[Add knowledge documents]
  C --> D[Run the document-review workflow]
  D --> E[Refresh the configuration periodically]

notes.objective: Configure custom instructions to establish tone, style, and output requirements for Project-specific use cases.
notes.title: What goes in custom instructions
notes.gist: Good Project instructions define Claude's role, the organisation's standards and the required output structure, so every deliverable matches without repetition.
points: Three elements: the role or function (e.g. certification curriculum specialist), the mandated standards (framework, style guide, terminology) and the prescribed output format (templates, rubric layout).
Tone and voice: state the brand voice explicitly; an overly formal default is fixed once here, for every chat.
Leaving format 'to Claude's judgement' or relying on per-chat prompts loses consistency; omitting the role loses perspective.
Keep instructions to the minimal set that fully defines expected behaviour; add an example of approved output where format matters.
Instructions, documents and Skills are selected per business requirement; not every Project needs all three.
notes.tip: The complete option names role, standards and format together; options that drop one element or defer it to individual chats are incomplete.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Role or function] --> D[Custom instructions]
  B[Standards and terminology] --> D
  C[Output format and template] --> D
  D --> E[Consistent deliverables in every chat]

notes.objective: Organize and structure reference documents within Projects to enable effective source attribution and information retrieval.
notes.title: Organise knowledge for retrieval and attribution
notes.gist: Upload the documents Claude should cite, name them clearly, group related material and reference them by name so answers trace back to sources.
points: Project knowledge is used across all chats in the Project; add the core working documents up front.
Use clear, descriptive filenames, group related content in one Project, and reference specific documents by name in prompts.

When knowledge approaches the context limit, the Project switches automatically to RAG mode: a project knowledge search tool retrieves the relevant parts, capacity grows up to 10x, quality is maintained.
Cached Project content counts less against usage limits when reused; caches expire after inactivity.
Ask for answers with citations to the source document and section so reviewers can verify attribution.
notes.tip: Questions about 'source attribution' and 'retrieval' reward named, well-organised documents in Project knowledge; pasting documents into each chat or relying on memory is wrong.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Collect reference documents] --> B[Descriptive filenames]
  B --> C[Upload to Project knowledge]
  C --> D{Over the context limit?}
  D -->|Yes| E[RAG search tool retrieves parts]
  D -->|No| F[Full documents in context]

notes.objective: Design Projects with appropriate access controls and isolation mechanisms to protect client data and maintain security boundaries across multiple deployments.
notes.title: Isolate clients with separate private Projects
notes.gist: One private Project per client or deployment keeps data, instructions and memory apart; sharing is explicit, and admins can restrict it.
points: Create a separate Project per client with its own knowledge, instructions and memory; never mix two clients' documents in one Project.
Visibility: 'Only people invited' (private) versus everyone in the organisation (public); chats stay private even in a public Project unless shared.
Access is granted per user or, on Enterprise, per group; removing a member revokes access; archiving does not change permissions.
Owners can turn off project sharing or public projects for the organisation, and on Enterprise per role.
Each Project's memory is separate; turn off 'Use account memory' to stop cross-Project context leaking.
notes.tip: The isolation answer is 'separate Projects, private visibility, explicit invitations'; one shared Project with instructions to keep clients apart is the trap.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Client A Project, private] --> C[Invited members only]
  B[Client B Project, private] --> D[Different members]
  C --> E[Own knowledge, instructions, memory]
  D --> E
  E --> F[Admin controls the sharing policy]

notes.objective: Integrate Skills with Projects to enhance workflow effectiveness and support ongoing operational processes.
notes.title: Skills bring procedures, Projects bring context
notes.gist: Skills are folders of instructions and scripts that Claude loads when relevant; pair them with a Project's static knowledge and instructions to run repeatable workflows.
points: Skills teach repeatable procedures (brand-formatted documents, an analysis method); Projects provide always-loaded background knowledge; custom instructions apply broadly; MCP connectors reach external data.
Progressive disclosure: Claude loads only the Skills relevant to the task, protecting the context window.
Anthropic Skills (Excel, Word, PowerPoint, PDF) run automatically when code execution and file creation is on; custom Skills are uploaded under Customize, Skills.
Before enabling a Skill from an unfamiliar vendor: read the bundled files and scripts, check dependencies and any external network calls; the main risks are prompt injection and data exfiltration.
Team and Enterprise owners can provision Skills organisation-wide, require review before publishing and turn on security scanning.
notes.tip: 'How should Skills be integrated' answers describe Skills as task-specific procedures complementing Project instructions and documents; trust questions want 'review the contents and verify the source' before activation.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Project: instructions and documents] --> C[Workflow run]
  B[Skill: procedure and scripts] --> C
  C --> D[Claude loads the Skill when relevant]
  D --> E[Consistent, repeatable output]

notes.objective: Select and configure appropriate Project components, including custom instructions, documents, and Skills, to address specific business requirements.
notes.title: Pick components by requirement
notes.gist: Match each business need to the component that solves it: instructions for behaviour, documents for facts, Skills for procedures, memory for continuity, connectors for live systems.
points: Consistent tone and format: custom instructions. Facts and sources: Project documents. A repeatable multi-step procedure: a Skill.
Continuity across chats without re-explaining: Project memory and chat search. Live external data: a connector (MCP), not a static upload.
A shared team repository of brand guidelines and templates used for months: a shared Project, not an artifact or per-chat uploads.
A technical documentation Project includes the style guide and product reference documents; unrelated material is left out to keep context focused.
Reassess the set when requirements change; add a component only when a need is real.
notes.tip: Distractors confuse artifacts (editable output) with knowledge management, or connectors (reactive retrieval) with a persistent knowledge base.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A{Need?} -->|Behaviour, tone, format| B[Custom instructions]
  A -->|Facts and sources| C[Project documents]
  A -->|Repeatable procedure| D[Skill]
  A -->|Continuity across chats| E[Project memory]
  A -->|Live external data| F[Connector]

notes.objective: Utilize Project Memory to maintain context and configuration across multiple conversations without requiring reconfiguration.
notes.title: Project memory keeps context between chats
notes.gist: Memory saves topics from your chats so new conversations start informed; each Project keeps its own memory, and you can review, edit, back up and switch it off.
points: Claude saves memory as individual topics as you chat; you can say 'remember this'; Settings, Memory lists everything and lets you edit or delete topics.
Each Project has its own memory, used alongside account memory but never another Project's; disable 'Use account memory' for full separation.
Maintain memory deliberately: back up before edits, review entries systematically, correct or remove obsolete ones, add missing context; do not wipe or disable it wholesale.
Chat search lets Claude pull relevant details from past conversations on paid plans; incognito chats and memory-off chats are excluded.
Sensitive topics are not stored unless you opt in; organisation owners can enable or disable memory for Team and Enterprise.
notes.tip: Memory maintenance questions want 'back up, then curate'; clearing everything, leaving it untouched or turning memory off are the distractors. Continuity across sessions without re-explaining is memory plus Projects.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Chat in a Project] --> B[Memory topics saved to the Project]
  B --> C[Next chat starts with context]
  C --> D[Review, edit, back up topics]
  D --> E[Account memory optional per Project]

summary.tests: Whether you can set up a Project properly: instructions first, documents organised for attribution, isolation per client, Skills for procedures, memory for continuity.
must_know: First action in a new Project: write the system-level custom instructions; then documents, then workflows.
Complete custom instructions state role, organisational standards and output format together.
Organise knowledge with descriptive filenames, grouped by topic, referenced by name; RAG mode activates automatically near the context limit with up to 10x capacity.
Isolation: one private Project per client, explicit invitations, separate memory; owners can restrict sharing.
Skills = repeatable procedures loaded when relevant; Projects = always-loaded knowledge; custom instructions = broad behaviour; MCP = external data.
Vet an unfamiliar Skill by reading its files, scripts, dependencies and network calls before enabling.
Memory: per-Project topics editable in Settings; maintain by backing up then curating; incognito and memory-off chats are excluded.
traps: Mixing clients in one Project with an instruction to keep them apart.
Fixing tone in the first message of every chat instead of in Project instructions.
Clearing or disabling memory instead of curating it, or treating an artifact as a knowledge base.

cards.q: First action when setting up a new Project for routine analytical tasks?
cards.a: Establish the system-level custom instructions; then add knowledge documents and start the workflows.

cards.q: Three elements of complete Project custom instructions for documentation work?
cards.a: Claude's role, the organisation's standards and terminology, and the prescribed output format or template.

cards.q: Claude is too formal in every new Project chat. Best fix?
cards.a: Put the desired tone in the Project's custom instructions so every chat starts with the right voice.

cards.q: How do you organise Project knowledge for retrieval and attribution?
cards.a: Descriptive filenames, related documents grouped in one Project, references to documents by name, answers with citations.

cards.q: What happens when Project knowledge exceeds the context limit?
cards.a: RAG mode turns on automatically: a project knowledge search tool retrieves relevant parts, capacity grows up to 10x, quality holds.

cards.q: Two clients with distinct security needs. How do you isolate them?
cards.a: Separate private Projects, each with its own knowledge, instructions, memory and explicitly invited members.

cards.q: Private versus public Project visibility?
cards.a: Private: only invited people. Public: everyone in the organisation can find it and start chats, but chats stay private unless shared.

cards.q: How do Skills differ from Projects and custom instructions?
cards.a: Skills are task-specific procedures loaded when relevant; Projects give always-loaded knowledge; custom instructions apply broadly to all chats.

cards.q: Two checks before enabling a Skill from an unfamiliar vendor?
cards.a: Read the bundled files, scripts and dependencies, and check for instructions that reach external network sources; confirm the source is trusted.

cards.q: What are the main risks of Skills?
cards.a: Prompt injection that makes Claude take unintended actions, and data exfiltration via malicious code or injected instructions.

cards.q: Two priorities in a Memory maintenance review?
cards.a: Back up existing memories before editing, then systematically correct or remove obsolete entries and add missing context.

cards.q: How is a Project's memory related to account memory?
cards.a: Each Project has its own memory used alongside account memory, never another Project's; turn off 'Use account memory' to isolate it.

cards.q: Which capability minimises re-introducing context when switching between AI platforms?
cards.a: Claude memory and chat search within Projects: context persists across sessions, so it need not be re-explained.

cards.q: Why revisit a Project configuration that still produces good output?
cards.a: Policies, terminology and reference materials evolve; refresh instructions and documents periodically, not only on quality drops.

cards.q: Trap: which components get confused with a knowledge base?
cards.a: Artifacts (editable output content) and connectors (reactive retrieval); a persistent shared knowledge base is a Project.
